author: Muḥammad Qāsim Firishtah; trans. and continued by Alexander Dow
publisher: T. Becket and P. A. De Hondt
frontispiece_type: serial imperial portraits: Shah Alam II in vol. I; Akbar in vol. II
artist_or_engraver: Josiah Taylor for the Shah Alam II engraving; second engraver to normalize
notes: Tufts and Christie's independently collate two engraved frontispieces. Modern scholarship identifies the vol. I image as Shah Alam II ('the present Emperor of Hindostan') after an original painting and the vol. II image as Jalaluddin Akbar. This edition therefore places Mughal sovereigns, not translator/historian Dow, in the frontispiece position.

author: Demetrius Cantemir; trans. Nicholas Tindal
work: The History of the Growth and Decay of the Othman Empire
artist_or_engraver: mezzotint engraver unresolved in current evidence
notes: Sotheby's and other rare-book collations identify a mezzotint portrait frontispiece of Cantemir, followed separately by a folding plan of Constantinople and 22 engraved portraits of Ottoman sultans (attributed in catalogue descriptions to C. Du Bosc). The visual opening authorizes the historian/eyewitness rather than an Ottoman ruler.

author: Thomas Maurice
work: The History of Hindostan; its Arts, and its Sciences
publisher: W. Bulmer and Co. for the author; sold by R. Faulder
frontispiece_type: comparative-religious/mythological frontispieces: Isis/Isa/Ceres in vol. I; Krishna triumphing over serpent in vol. II
notes: A detailed 1795-98 copy collation identifies vol. I Plate I, facing the title page, as 'Isis Omnia, or universal nature personified, the Indian Isa, and Grecian Ceres'; vol. II Plate I, facing its title page, depicts Creeshna/Krishna trampling the serpent. Christie's independently records two engraved frontispieces and fifteen other engraved plates. These frontispieces frame historical comparison through comparative mythology rather than portraiture.
